title: A Book of Maps for You
author: Lourdes Heuer, illustrated by Maxwell Eaton III
text: Kids often have to do map units in school, and at first this book seems very much in that vein. Here’s a map of rooms in a home. Here’s a map of the street. The occasional pirate map. Still, as you read, a story slowly begins to emerge. Who is making these maps? Why? The unexpected gut punch of an ending gives a surprising resonance to what, at the start, just seemed like a straightforward map compendium. It turns out that this is less a book about the beauty of mapmaking (though that certainly plays a role) and more about moving from one home to another. Ideal for both reminding children about what they love and are leaving, and how much they may love the place where they are going. Seeming simplicity with an emotional core. (For ages 4 to 8)

title: Baldwin: A Love Story
author: Nicholas Boggs
text: The book is massive at 720 pages – but how else can anyone properly summarize James Baldwin’s love life and the effects it had on his creative process? Baldwin: A Love Story is a biography organized by the four men with whom Baldwin had his most significant relationships, until his death in 1987. Each was a turbulent affair, and several took the writer across the globe. Portions of the deeply researched book are told in Baldwin’s own words through excerpts of correspondence he kept with friends, family and, of course, his lovers.

author: Fady Joudah
text: A wordless title is incredibly fitting for this National Book Award finalist poetry collection that is felt more than it is read. Fady Joudah writes of the horror faced by Palestinians as they live, love and die through war and violence against them. The poem “Dedication” lists the many whom these poems are dedicated to. “To the martyrs who witness from above, and the living who witness on the ground. To those who will be killed on the last day of the war. To those who will be killed on the first day after the war ends. To those who succumb in the humanitarian window of horror. An hour before the pause, a minute after.” The collection shows us the world through Palestinian eyes at a time when such a worldview is most needed.

title: A Short Walk Through a Wide World
author: Douglas Westerbeke
text: It’s the year 1885, in Paris, when 9-year-old Aubry Tourvel encounters a mysterious, wooden puzzle ball: It may be a blessing or a curse, but it most definitely changes her life. Now she needs to keep moving forever; too long in any one town and she will bleed to death. So her life is all travel and adventure, and through her we wonder at the richness of the globe’s markets, towns, forests and deserts. Over many decades, she meets all types of kind and curious people – as well as cruel and uncaring ones. Sometimes Aubry enjoys quick communion with strangers. Other times, she is surrounded but desperately lonely. This is a ravishing, deeply human book that’s in love with the world, with people, with the new – and yet is infused with a deep, futile longing for home.

title: The School for Good Mothers: A Novel
author: Jessamine Chan
text: Should the government have a say in what makes someone a good mother? Jessamine Chan’s debut novel is a disturbing and thought-provoking look at government involvement in child welfare. The main character, Frida, is an overwhelmed single mom. After leaving her toddler home alone, Frida is sent to a dystopian facility designed to rehabilitate mothers. The program wears the women down so much that it’s nearly impossible for them to meet the government’s standard of near-perfection to regain custody of their children. It’s neither light nor cheery, but The School for Good Mothers stays with you long after the final page.

title: Vulture
author: Phoebe Greenwood
text: I grew up in Gaza and covered it until I left in 2017. This novel reminded me that fiction can reveal more about the people who bring us the news than reportage ever can. It shows the relentless stress of the work, the creeping numbness, and the small moments of humanity that survive in spite of everything. I was struck by how accurately it captures the younger version of myself: ambitious, chasing the biggest and riskiest stories, never stopping long enough to understand what that drive was doing to me. Vulture grasps the moral and personal cost of that pursuit with remarkable clarity. Its emotional center is the relationship between the Western correspondent and the local journalist, two people trying to report honestly in a place sealed off and constantly in danger. The novel also exposes the gendered hierarchy of war reporting, where young women are taken seriously only when catastrophe surrounds them. By the end, it reminded me what it meant to live that life and why I stepped outside it.

title: An Oral History of Atlantis: Stories
author: Ed Park
text: Although this is his first short-story collection, Ed Park told Lit Hub that the stories were actually written over a span of about 25 years. No surprise, then, that readers will recognize the same playful wit and eclectic, occasionally challenging style that animate his two previous novels, including the 2024 Pulitzer Prize finalist, Same Bed Different Dreams. But unlike that book, which pulls from Korea’s past for a grandly wrought alternative history, the stories in Atlantis live squarely in our own absurd present, a workaday wonderland where lives can be told in sleep-medication side effects and Internet login passwords.

title: The Feather Detective: Mystery, Mayhem, and the Magnificent Life of Roxie Laybourne
author: Chris Sweeney
text: Forensic ornithology is real, and Roxie Laybourne made it happen. This painstaking biography traces the ornithologist’s Smithsonian career from early days restoring samples to being the world’s best bird identifier, assisting with everything from poaching investigations to NASA flights. Though not always comfortable under the pressure of working with law enforcement, Laybourne was an indomitable force, and her passion for birds – through investigation, teaching and conservation – is evident on every page. For those who love niche stories of nature, science and social history, The Feather Detective offers a timely account of a fascinating – and peculiar – ecosystem: one woman, and lots and lots of birds.

title: A Constellation Of Vital Phenomena: A Novel
author: Anthony Marra
text: The title is hard to wrap your mind around. It comes from a medical textbook’s definition of “life.” Set during Chechnya’s wars for independence from Russia, Anthony Marra’s novel begins in a small village where a young girl’s father has just been taken away by government troops. Her rescuer, the village doctor, seeks refuge in a barely functioning urban hospital run by a brilliant surgeon — a still-young woman whose emotions have been stripped bare by war. These and the other characters whose lives run through this story of life in the midst of war are among the most memorable I have ever encountered. They will break your heart and keep you reading.

title: Not a Speck of Light
author: Laird Barron
text: Laird Barron’s work comes from a place in which crime and cosmic horror collide with stellar results. The haunting memories of a serial killer, an elderly couple who learn to live with the thing that inhabits their attic, and the lingering effects of sinister childhood games are just some of the things readers will find in this superbly written collection from one of the best contemporary purveyors of Vantablack-dark speculative fiction.

title: The Nightmare Box and Other Stories
author: Cynthia Gómez
text: This was hands down my favorite horror anthology of 2024. The stories are loudly and proudly Latinx, queer, feminist and working-class. You’ll encounter Black Panthers and vampires, witches and magical clothes, brave activists and cops who get what’s coming to them. Longtime San Francisco Bay Area residents will love picking up the references to local sights – places that never hit the tourist tours or the big bestsellers. Of the 12 stories in the anthology, the eponymous story is the one I think about the most. Set in 1970, the piece is about a woman named Serena who can create custom-made nightmares. She’s forced to work against the interests of some local activists and decides to resist in the only way she knows how.

title: Tangier in the Rain
author: Fabien Grolleau, illustrated by Abdel de Bruxelles and translated by David Christensen
text: Recounting Matisse’s two visits to Tangier, Morocco, between 1912 and 1913, this sumptuous graphic novel belies a mordant critique – by showing how the French master perceives the North African landscape as a place to be exploited aesthetically, rather than a country with its complex truths. Since it rains almost nonstop during his initial trip, Matisse has to find ways to reconcile with the intemperate environment. Tangier in the Rain comically illustrates Matisse’s dependence on so-called secondary characters, such as Madame Matisse, his headstrong model Zorah and local Moroccans, who greatly contribute to Matisse’s artistic vision but are not adequately credited by posterity.

title: The Things They Fancied
author: Molly Young
text: The only thing that might’ve been more fun than breezing through this NSFW zine is researching it. In the early days of the pandemic, Molly Young spent two voyeuristic weeks immersed in the ridiculous obsessions of the rich. Mini chapters include countryside manors, French teeth, pineapples, pubic mist, pet squirrels, luxury fragrance. With the right social marketing, she suggests, we’ll fall for anything. Young diagnoses us as the gluttons we are: “People spend money on the dumbest s*** … rich people just spend a lot more of it.” While I – like many – was stuck inside during the bleakest of summers, Young’s wry romp into how the other half lives, today and throughout history, was a fizzy tonic. I emerged grateful for modern amenities like fresh produce, dentistry, bleach and toilets. Recommended if you fancy: Airbnb cottage getaways, JSTOR rabbitholes, Marie Antoinette, The Favourite, sneering at the 1%.

title: Blackouts
author: Justin Torres
text: Blackouts is an immersive experience. This National Book Award winner contains photographs, illustrations and handwritten letters – ephemera that help tell the story of an early 20th-century lesbian researcher and activist named Jan Gay. Justin Torres embeds her real-life story (complete with cameos from Andy Warhol, Emma Goldman and Martin Scorsese) in a fictional (or is it?) dialogue between a dying man named Juan Gay and a young unnamed narrator. The book is mysterious, sexy and layered, and as soon as I finished it, I wanted to go back and read it again.

title: The Hacienda
author: Isabel Cañas
text: I’m a sucker for Gothic novels, and I’ve been loving the trend of Gothics that take place somewhere unexpected (i.e., not Europe). The Hacienda is a story that takes us to, well, a hacienda – in a remote Mexican town in the 1820s, not long after the War of Independence. The protagonist, Beatriz, moves to her new husband’s large estate, eager to escape the rejection, poverty and tragedy that she’s suffered in Mexico City. What she finds instead is a ridiculously haunted house inhabited by some equally haunted-seeming people – including those meant to be closest to her.

title: The Magician: A Novel
author: Colm Tóibín
text: Colm TóibÍn’s magnificent biographical novel about Thomas Mann encompasses the full sweep of the German Nobel Prize-winner’s life, including his carefully repressed homosexuality, the genesis of major works like the story “Death in Venice” and The Magic Mountain, and the devastating rise of Nazism, which sent him, his wealthy, secular Jewish wife, and their large, often ungovernable brood of artistic offspring into exile in Switzerland and the U.S. With its intertwined portraits of a deep, complicated writer and a world that changed beyond recognition in his lifetime, The Magician should appeal to history buffs as well as literary mavens.

links.text: All Sides Weekend: Books- 'The Magician'

title: Our Lake
author: Angie Kang
text: How do we carry the memory of loved ones after they’ve passed? Angie Kang’s beautiful book explores this question by following two brothers returning to a lake where they used to swim with their father. There is an undercurrent of melancholy to swimming now without their father, but together the brothers find the strength to dive back in – and in doing so, they create new memories that help keep the old ones alive. Like the still surface of a lake, this book appears quiet but contains incredible depth, immersing readers in an experience that holds heartache and joy in equal measure. (For ages 4 to 8)

title: Becoming Ghost: Poetry
author: Cathy Linh Che
text: In 1976, the author’s parents, then Vietnam War survivors living in a refugee camp in the Philippines, were able to earn relatively good wages by becoming extras in Francis Coppola’s Apocalypse Now. They mostly played civilian casualties or Vietcong snipers who were background scenery or “ghosts” in the director’s operatic but ultimately hollow Vietnam parable. Cathy Linh Che restructures lines in Coppola’s filmscript to create dramatic monologues that lend texture and corporeality to her parents’ cinema-worthy history. Her approach is both poignant and humble. While wishing to rectify the past by serving as a vessel for her parents’ voices, Che is fully aware that such an attempt at capturing their elusive narratives is still a scripted effort. The collection was a finalist for the National Book Award.

title: You Gotta Be You: How to Embrace This Messy Life and Step Into Who You Really Are
author: Brandon Kyle Goodman
text: What if fitting in wasn’t worth the energy, the pain? Who would you be if you could shove off other people’s expectations? Brandon Kyle Goodman, who is Black, queer and nonbinary, has done a lot of work trying to figure that out for themself, and they’re sharing all they’ve learned – the highs, the lows, the mess – in this book. How can we show up better to love others, while respecting our own boundaries so we can better love ourselves? We laughed, we cried, we cry-laughed — and by the end, felt better about bringing our full selves to everything we do.

title: Glitter Everywhere! Where It Came From, Where It's Found & Where It's Going
author: Chris Barton, illustrated by Chaaya Prabhat
text: Why did the European Union officially ban loose glitter in 2023? We think we’ve found the answer. Everyone’s favorite microplastic gets a book of its own as Chris Barton digs deep to show everything about the sparkly substance, from its invention and ties to the LGBTQ+ community to its devastating effect on the environment. Original research digs into who created the first glitter and what we can do to create a sustainable version in the future. Love glitter? Great! Hate glitter? Even better! Here’s a book that can truly appeal to both sides of this eternal debate. (For ages 5 to 9)

title: Monster Portraits
author: Sofia Samatar, illustrated by Del Samatar
text: Sofia and Del Samatar are siblings, and Monster Portraits is a collaboration between her writing and his art, resulting in a gorgeous collection of related vignettes musing on the nature of monsters and monstrosity. Not a bestiary so much as an antibestiary – one that considers every fantastical creature represented as a person to be encountered – Monster Portraits explores and unpacks thoughts about diaspora, race, travel and inheritance in the same sharp, spare, heartbreaking prose that characterized Sofia Samatar’s The Winged Histories.

links.text: Siblings On A Strange Journey In 'Monster Portraits'

title: Everybody Counts: A Counting Story From 0 To 7.5 Billion
author: Kristin Roskifte, translated by Siân Mackie
text: A seek-and-find book for the 21st century. Every person has a story, but can you figure out what those stories are? It’s a book that’s part puzzle, part ode to humanity. What appears at first to be a simple Norwegian counting book takes a strange turn. “Five people in a family. Three of them love reading. One of them is secretly in love.” Expect a grand romance, a crook, innocent people in jail and more! Shows that anyone you see in this great big wonderful world may have a life that you are not privy to. (For ages 4 to 8)

title: Exhalation: Stories
author: Ted Chiang
text: A warning letter from the future. A museum exhibit card describing the mechanization of nurturing. An exploration of emergent artificial intelligence. The stories in Ted Chiang’s newest short story collection are tightly focused dramas of individuals whom the future has struck like a wave, or a bomb. And whether the “future” is tomorrow or 100 years ago (as seen from someone witnessing it from 101 years ago), it has the weight of inexorability to it. Tomorrow comes whether we want it to or not. The world changes no matter how tightly we cling to yesterday. And Chiang writes often (almost always) with an understanding that nothing we do, nothing he does, nothing any of his characters do, can change that.

links.text: Take A Breath And Dive Into 'Exhalation'

title: Psychopomp & Circumstance
author: Eden Royce
text: Set in an alternate, magical, post-Reconstruction South Carolina, this Southern gothic novella delves into generational secrets and self-realization. Phaedra St. Margaret and her socialite mother have never gotten along, what with Phee’s stubborn refusal to behave like a “proper” young lady. After her estranged aunt dies, Phee heads from New Charleston to the small town of Horizon in a cart pulled by a hippocamp to plan her aunt’s homegoing. Buried memories, mysteriously locked rooms and strange spirits lurk in the corners of Aunt Cleo’s home in this haunting story.

title: Who Is Government?: The Untold Story of Public Service
author: Michael Lewis (editor)
text: Thousands of unsung heroes in the government are making life better for Americans. But because of bureaucracies being made up of bureaucrats, we rarely hear those stories. This book showcases them. Like a coal-mining safety official who helped the U.S. reach zero mine-collapse deaths. Or the man who has led the National Cemetery Administration to the top of the American Customer Satisfaction Index. As the federal government is in its biggest shake-up in a generation, it’s worth learning about where the bright spots are.

title: The Vixen: A Novel
author: Francine Prose
text: I confess I almost stopped reading this after the first chapter. It’s loosely based on Ethel and Julius Rosenberg, the American couple executed during the Cold War for being suspected Soviet spies, and I feared it would be depressingly serious. Who needs that these days? But I pushed on, and it became another book entirely. Part coming-of-age story, part romance and part comedy, it’s alternately poignant and hilarious, with wonderful insights into family, society, class and ethics, and wry commentary on the fragile egos of writers. It’s filled with life lessons and, in a bonus, contains an intentionally cheesy novel-within-a-novel. As Francine Prose told me: “Writing badly on purpose is so much fun!”
